prompts.target: pain and the story about it
prompts.title: The toothache at the bus stop
prompts.text: A character is waiting at a bus stop with a tooth that has started to ache. Write the scene in 400 to 700 words so that a reader can feel two separate things: the ache itself, and the story the character begins telling about what it means. Leave out the word "pain", the dentist and the cost. A stranger interrupts once, and the interruption must neither ease the ache nor answer the story.
prompts.done_when: You can quote one passage that is only the ache and another that is only the story.
prompts.move: two separate layers: the ache, and the story about it
prompts.why: B069 separates a painful sensation from the extra suffering added by reacting to it. The scene keeps those layers apart on the page and leaves the writer to decide what the story does to the ache.

prompts.target: help, and who gets a say
prompts.title: The mended gate
prompts.text: Someone has fixed their neighbour's gate without being asked. Write 500 to 800 words that begin the first time the neighbour tries to open it. Each of them has a good reason for wanting the gate to work a certain way, and neither may state that reason in a speech. Let the argument happen through the latch, the hinges and what their hands do. Stop on a question one of them asks that the other cannot yet answer.
prompts.done_when: Both reasons can be inferred from action alone, and the last line is an unanswered question.
prompts.move: argue through the latch, the hinges and the hands
prompts.why: B099 asks what help the other person would actually welcome; R077 treats a person's say over their own life as formed in relationships. A repaired gate puts a kind act and someone's autonomy in the same doorway.

prompts.target: not knowing how events will turn out
prompts.title: Three people and a changed timetable
prompts.text: Overnight, someone has altered a bus timetable. Write three short scenes, 600 to 900 words in all, each following a different person who relies on it. In the first, the change looks like good luck; in the second it wrecks a plan; the third person cannot tell which it is. Nothing in the telling may rank the three. End in the middle of the third person's decision.
prompts.done_when: Three people are affected differently, nothing ranks them, and the last decision is still open.
prompts.move: three scenes, three different readings of the same change
prompts.why: D110 retells the old story in which every event is judged from the middle of a longer chain. CO068 asks where a belief runs out of evidence. Three partial views give the writer room to stay inside not-knowing.

prompts.title: Worn smooth
prompts.text: Pick the nearest thing that has been worn smooth by use. Write a twelve-line poem that leaves it three times, once for a memory, once for a plan, once for a worry, and comes back each time through a different physical detail of the object: a weight, a temperature, an edge. Do not use the words "attention", "focus" or "mind".
prompts.done_when: Count three departures and three returns, each return through a new physical detail.
prompts.anchor: an object worn smooth by use
prompts.why: AT019 treats the return, not the absence of distraction, as the skill. The poem builds that cycle into its shape and never has to name it.

prompts.title: Packing for one night
prompts.text: Write a poem as the packing list for one night away. Each line names an item and the need it meets. Somewhere past the middle the list quietly starts to include things nobody needs. Do not announce the change; let only the items show it. The final line must be something that weighs nothing.
prompts.done_when: A reader can find the line where need turns into want by the items alone.
prompts.move: show the shift through the items, not through comment
prompts.why: D019 reads contentment as knowing when a need is met and stopping there. A list makes sufficiency concrete, and it leaves open whether the extra items are folly, comfort or love.

prompts.title: When the machine switches off
prompts.text: A machine in the building you are in has just switched off: a fridge, a lift motor, a fan. Write ten to eighteen lines that begin with what you hear stop, then move to something in your own body that was braced without your knowing, then outward again to a thing in the room you had not noticed. Leave out "silence" and "quiet", and keep the machine's name out until the last line, if it appears at all.
prompts.done_when: The poem goes room, body, room, and the last detail is new.
prompts.move: move from the room to the body and back out
prompts.why: B186 treats rest as part of the work rather than its failure. The poem looks for the moment when rest is noticed, not for a claim that stillness is always restful.

prompts.title: The number you check
prompts.text: Choose a number you check about yourself: steps, savings, hours, followers, words written. In 600 to 900 words, describe one day it told you something true about how you were doing and another day it hid something. Then argue for what the number cannot count by describing one hour that left no trace in it. End on the question you would now write next to the number.
prompts.done_when: Two particular days, one uncounted hour, and a closing question that is about how you use the number.
prompts.move: argue for what the number cannot count
prompts.why: BE011 reports that tracking tends to help behaviour; D079 questions conventional measures of success. Holding both lets the essay take the number seriously and still ask what a good life includes that it misses.

prompts.title: What the sting wanted
prompts.text: Think of someone whose good fortune made you wince. In 500 to 800 words, first set down what you actually know about their situation, then what you only imagine. Next, say what the sting was pointing at, naming the want as an object or an activity, not a rank or a status. End with what you would do this week if the want deserved to be taken seriously, and what you would do if it did not.
prompts.done_when: Knowledge and imagination are in separate paragraphs, and the want is named without any rank or status words.
prompts.move: name the want as an object or activity
prompts.why: AF055 describes research on benign and malicious envy as differing in the motivation they produce. The prompt asks what the feeling points toward and leaves open whether following it is wise.

prompts.title: A direction you cannot finish
prompts.text: Begin with the words "For the next ten years I am walking toward" and complete them with a direction, not a destination: something you could never finish arriving at. In 600 to 900 words, bring in one concrete thing from last week that was on that route and one that was not but felt as if it were. Close with what you would have to stop doing to stay on the route.
prompts.done_when: The opening names a direction that cannot be completed, and the ending names something you would give up.
prompts.move: sort one real event onto the route and one off it
prompts.why: PP025 treats purpose as a direction to pursue, not a goal to reach; MO058 looks at letting go of goals that cannot be reached. Together they ask what a chosen direction costs.

prompts.title: The practical thing
prompts.text: Recall a time someone came to you in a bad stretch and did something small and practical instead of saying anything wise. In 300 to 500 words, say what they did, in order, with the objects involved. Hold back how it felt until the last two sentences; there, say what the act did that words could not, or admit it did nothing you can name. If no memory fits, write the scene for an invented person and label it fiction.
prompts.done_when: The act is in order with its objects, and feeling is held to the last two sentences.
prompts.anchor: objects used in a small practical act
prompts.move: postpone feeling to the last two sentences
prompts.why: A068 holds that friendship shows in presence during misfortune; B099 asks what help is actually welcome. Remembering a practical act keeps care concrete and avoids a speech about it.

prompts.title: A stranger with your name
prompts.text: Find something you wrote or signed at least ten years ago. In 400 to 700 words, read it as if it came from a stranger who shares your name: what does the document seem to want? Then say one thing the stranger got right about you, and one thing you would not recognise in yourself now. Write about the document first and bring yourself in only in the final paragraph. If nothing like it survives, skip this prompt or write it as clearly labelled fiction.
prompts.done_when: One thing the stranger got right, one you no longer recognise, and yourself absent until the final paragraph.
prompts.anchor: an old signed or written document
prompts.move: read your own document as a stranger
prompts.why: E083 holds identity as both continuity and change, and CO010 treats thinking as story-making. An old document tests the story against something written before the story was settled.

prompts.title: What a camera would have caught
prompts.text: Recall a small quarrel in which you were fairly sure you were right. In 300 to 500 words, write only what a camera could have recorded: what was said and who stood where. Then add one paragraph listing three assumptions you made in that moment that no camera could have shown. Leave who was right unsettled. Choose a low-stakes memory; if none comes, hand the quarrel to two invented people and say that you did.
prompts.done_when: A camera-only account, then exactly three assumptions in a separate paragraph, and no verdict.
prompts.move: separate the recordable from the assumed
prompts.why: B140 asks what has actually been heard and what the listener supplied; A060 turns on whether someone acted knowingly. The exercise separates what happened from what was assumed about it, before any question of forgiving.
